title: 北朝鮮非難の国連決議 米国が棄権
body: 人権問題を扱う国連総会の第3委員会は18日、北朝鮮の人権侵害を強く非難する決議案を、日本を含む95カ国の賛成多数で採択した。2016年以降は「無投票」で決まっていたが、決議案が国際刑事裁判所（ICC）を関与させる可能性にも触れているため、ICCへの圧力を強める米国が投票を要求した上で「棄権」票を投じた。【あわせて読みたい】制裁下のICCに加盟国ができること　オランダの国際法学者から提案米国は決議案について「安全保障理事会がICCへの付託の検討も含め、引き続き関与することを期待する」としている点に反発。ICCは「脅威」だと主張し、この言及の削除を求めてきた。トランプ政権はICCの「解体」を掲げ、赤根智子所長らを制裁対象に指定している。一方、棄権はあくまでこの点に異議を唱えたものだとし、北朝鮮の人権状況は「極めて深刻」で「懸念は共有している」とも述べた。■拉致被害者の帰国要求も決議案の採択は22年連続。日本人を含むすべての拉致被害者の即時帰国を求める内容も盛り込まれている。米国は例年、強い賛意を示す「共同提案国」も務めていた。反対は北朝鮮、中国、ロシア、ベトナムなど14カ国、棄権は米国を含め58カ国だった。米国はこの日、ミャンマーの少数派イスラム教徒ロヒンギャや、ウクライナ国内のロシアによる占領地をめぐる類似の決議でも、ICCへの言及があったことを理由に棄権した。（ニューヨーク＝田中恭太）

title: 米史上初 黒人の下院議長誕生へ
body:
【ワシントン共同】米中間選挙で勝利した民主党は18日、来年1月招集の新議会の議長候補に下院党トップで黒人のハキーム・ジェフリーズ院内総務（56）を選出した。新議会で民主党は多数派を握るため、米史上初めて黒人の下院議長が誕生することが確実になった。下院議長は大統領権限の継承順位が副大統領に次ぐ2位の要職。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
米メディアによると、民主党会派内の無記名投票で対抗馬はおらず、251人がジェフリーズ氏を支持し、来年1月の本会議の議長選で当選に必要な218票を大きく上回った。急進左派の政治団体「米国民主社会主義者」（DSA）に所属する一部が反対した。ジェフリーズ氏はニューヨーク出身。弁護士や州下院議員を経て2013年に連邦下院議員に就任。23年にペロシ元下院議長の後任として党院内総務を引き継ぎ、民主、共和両党、上下両院を通じて黒人初の党議会指導部トップとなった。

title: 市民デモ相次ぐ仏 警官が抗議デモ
body: 市民の抗議デモが相次ぐフランスで今度は警察官たちが劣悪な労働環境の改善を求めて抗議デモを行いました。【動画】フランスで全国一斉ストライキ　物価高に抗議　57万人超参加　エッフェル塔も休館18日、パリの内務省前に集まったのは数百人の警察官たちです。フランス各地では9月以降、学生や労働者らによる抗議デモが相次いでいます。デモに便乗して破壊や略奪を行う集団を警戒し警察官などが厳しく取り締まっています。警察の労働組合幹部によりますと、現場の疲労がピークに達し、17日だけで機動隊員500人以上が体調不良などで医師の診察を受けたということです。警察の労働組合幹部「私たちは月曜から週6～7日働いています。通常12時間の勤務シフトが、時には19時間にも及びます。警察官は30キロもの重い装備品を身につけ、1日に20～30キロを移動しています。（デモ隊の一部と）いたちごっこのような状態になるため、現場は本当に非常に厳しい状況です」警察の労働組合は政府に対して、労働環境の抜本的な見直しや2019年から据え置かれている「危険手当」の増額などを求めています。

title: 熊本で震度5弱 住民「夜は怖い」
body:
19日午前2時22分ごろ、熊本県で最大震度5弱を観測する地震が発生しました。【写真】8月1日以来の震度5弱…熊本地震の一連の活動「もうやめてほしい」「夜は怖い」住宅の瓦が落下する被害も
震源地は、天草・芦北地方で、震源の深さは約10km、地震の規模を示すマグニチュードは5.7と推定されます。震度5弱を観測したのは、水俣市、芦北町、津奈木町球磨村、あさぎり町。震度4を観測したのは、八代市、人吉市、上天草市宇城市、天草市、美里町氷川町、錦町、多良木町、山江村です。熊本県内で震度5弱を観測したのは、8月1日以来で、気象台によると、7月の地震の一連の活動ということです。気象台は、揺れの強かった地域では、今後1週間程度さらに強い揺れをもたらす地震が発生する可能性があるため、注意を呼びかけています。未明の地震を受けて、水俣市と球磨村で全域に避難指示が、津奈木町で高齢者等避難が出されています。また、交通機関などにも影響が出ています。肥薩おれんじ鉄道は始発から八代ー出水間で運転を見合わせています。九州新幹線は8本が運休し、新八代－出水の一部区間では速度を落として運転しています。高速道路は、九州自動車道が八代ICー人吉IC間で通行止め、南九州自動車道が八代JCTー日奈久IC間で通行止めになっています。■「長い横揺れ…」震度5弱の町では震度5弱を観測した津奈木町では、繰り返し襲う地震に不安の声が聞かれました。住民は「10秒ほどの長い横揺れを感じた」「7月の震度5強の地震よりも強い揺れを感じた」と話していました。なかには、何度も続く余震に寝られなかったという声も聞かれました。一部の建物にも被害が出ています。津奈木町の住宅では、2階の屋根瓦が落下しました。住人は「前回は家の中の被害は多かったが、今回は外。前回の地震のダメージも蓄積しているのではないか」と話していました。日奈久断層帯の“割れ残り”があるとされ、最大震度7が予想されている地域で「心の準備はしていたが、もうやめてほしい」という声も多く聞かれました。■「夜は怖い」仮設団地の住民　不安の声7月の地震で震度7を観測した氷川町は、今回、震度4の揺れに襲われました。氷川町によりますと、今回の地震による住宅の倒壊やけが人の情報は入っていませんが、仮設団地で暮らす住民からは不安の声が聞かれました。（住民）「また大きなのが来るかもしれないから不安ですね、夜は怖いですね。昼間だと見えているけど」「ガタガタガタとプレハブにいるから、特に揺れる。もう来てほしくない」氷川町の吉本仮設団地に住民は、大きな横揺れを感じたと話していました。7月の地震後に開設された町内の3つの避難所には、今も114人が避難しています。復興に向けて少しずつ歩みを進める中での地震に、住民は不安を隠しきれない状況です。

title: 2人死亡事故 容疑者勤務先を捜索
body: 神奈川県海老名市の交差点で13日に女性2人が大型トラックにはねられて死亡した事故で、神奈川県警は19日午前、自動車運転死傷処罰法違反（過失運転致死）と道路交通法違反（ひき逃げ）容疑で逮捕した会社員の会田誠容疑者（49）=相模原市緑区中野=の勤務先の運送会社「シンワロジスティクス」（相模原市緑区）など関係先に家宅捜索に入った。【写真】走り屋「聖地」を封鎖した神奈川県警の「挟み撃ち作戦」県警は、会田容疑者の勤務日誌を押収するなどし、事故当時の勤務実態や運行管理に問題がなかったかを調べる方針。会田容疑者は逮捕時「私が事故を起こしたという道路付近を通過したことは間違いありませんが、事故についてはまったくわかりません」などと話し、容疑を否認したという。海老名署によると、事故は13日午後3時10分ごろ発生。会田容疑者が運転する大型トラックが海老名市下今泉2丁目の交差点で、横断歩道を歩いて渡っていた女性2人をはねて、そのまま逃走。2人は現場で死亡が確認され、県警が身元の確認を進めている。捜査関係者によると、会田容疑者は事故当時、大型トラックで配送業務を終え、帰社途中だったという。事故の数時間後、この大型トラックが同社内に駐車されているのを県警が発見し、押収した。

title: 日中首脳が握手 会談は見送りへ
body: アジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に出席するため、中国・深圳を訪れている高市早苗首相は18日、議長を務める中国の習近平国家主席と会議開幕の記念撮影に臨み、握手を交わした。昨年11月の台湾有事を巡る高市氏の国会答弁をきっかけに日中関係が冷え込んで以降、両首脳が対面で顔を合わせるのは初めて。対面自体は昨年10月の韓国での首脳会談以来、2回目。【一覧】安倍氏や石破氏の時は?　APECでの日中巡る出来事高市氏は東南アジア諸国連合（ASEAN）関連首脳会議を終え、18日午後にフィリピン・マニラから深圳に到着。空港での中国による歓迎セレモニーは簡素だった。習氏との握手と記念撮影は夜の夕食会前に行われた。高市氏は出迎えた習氏と握手した際に話しかけ、習氏は温和な表情で応じた。APEC首脳会議は19日まで行われるが、期間中、高市氏と習氏の正式な会談は実施されない見通し。昨秋以来、日中両政府間でハイレベルの会談は開かれていない。中国側は対話の条件として、高市氏の国会答弁の撤回や是正を求めている。マニラで17日に開かれたASEANプラス3（日中韓）首脳会議では、中国の李強首相に代わって出席した張柱・農業農村相に高市氏が英語であいさつし、握手する場面もあった。【深圳・野間口陽】

title: トランプ氏 露大統領と個別会談へ
body: [ワシントン １８日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は１９日、ア‌ジア太平洋経済協力会⁠議（ＡＰＥＣ）首脳会議が開催されている中国で、ロ​シアのプーチン大統領と個別会談を行う‌見通し。米ロ両国の当局者が１８日明らかにした。米当局‌者は会談の予‌定を確認しつ​つも、それ以上の詳細には踏み‌込まなかった。１９日には中国の習近平国家‌主席も交​えた米中ロ首脳会談も‌予定されている。ロシアのインタフ⁠ァクス通信によると、ロシアのペスコフ大統領報道官は、１９日に⁠予定される米ロ首​脳会‌談で本格的な交渉は行われないだろうとの認識を示した。⁠また、ロシアのウシャ⁠コフ大統領補佐官（外交担当）⁠によると、米ロ会談はAPEC首脳会議の本‌会合⁠後に開かれ、両国代表​団の数人が出席する見通しという。

title: 米 ベネズエラと軍事協力で合意
body: [カラカス １８日 ロイター] - ヘグセス米国防長官は１８日、ベネズエラとの軍事協力に関する新たな合意を‌発表した。米軍の特殊部隊が１月にマドゥロ大統⁠領を拘束し退陣させて以降、ヘグセス氏にとって初めての同国訪問となる。ヘグセス氏は首都カラカス​でロドリゲス暫定大統領と会見し、合意は共同訓練や情報共有など、両国の軍事協力の幅‌広い分野を対象としていると説明。ロドリゲス氏は、今回の合意が「共通の脅威」への対処に寄与し、‌ベネズエラ軍の訓練を強化‌することになると語った。ヘグセス氏は、協​力によって麻薬密売組織に対する共同行動が大幅に強化される‌とし、こうした組織に向けて「おまえたちを追い詰め、見つけ出し、殺害す‌る」と述べた。ヘグセス氏​は中南米歴訪の最初の訪問地としてカラカス‌に立ち寄った。１８日にはコロンビアを訪れ、軍事装備品を引き渡すほか、⁠同国政府と安全保障協力について協議する予定だ。同氏は８月、コロンビアの武装組織に対する共同攻撃の可能性に言及していた。トラン⁠プ米大統領の中南米政策は、当初の重点​だったパナマ運河‌から、対象を大幅に広げている。米軍が２０２５年に麻薬密輸に関与した疑いのある船舶への攻撃を開始して以降、２００人以上が死亡し⁠た。カラカスでの集会で演説したヘグセス氏は、米⁠州全域で米国の優位性を主張する１９世紀のモンロー主義とトランプ氏⁠の名前を掛け合わせた「ドンロー主義」に言及。「これがドンロー主義‌だ。⁠ベネズエラはこの地域で最も攻撃的な脅威から、米国​と共に軍を再建する従順な安全保障上のパートナーへと変わった」と述べた。

title: 日本車の部品 一部共通化する方針
body:
日本の自動車業界が、メーカーの垣根を越えて素材や部品の一部を共通化する方針を固めたことが18日、分かった。日本自動車工業会（自工会）が、製造に使う鉄や樹脂の一部で種類や規格を統一する。コスト削減や開発期間の短縮につながる取り組みで、メーカー側は米中勢が先行する次世代車の開発に投資を振り向けられるようになる。【写真】中国企業に買われた「東芝ブランド」その後
ほかに共通化するのは電子機器のケーブルを束ねた「ワイヤーハーネス」と呼ばれる部品。自工会は自動車部品の業界団体と連携し、徐々に共通化の領域を広げていく考えだ。自工会は昨年12月、2026年度に対処すべきテーマの一つに、部品や素材の共通化を挙げていた。ただ自動車業界は大手メーカーを頂点に、系列の部品会社などが連なるピラミッド構造で、考え方の違いなどから議論は難航していたという。業界には電動化や自動運転技術の開発といった「100年に1度」の転換期が訪れている。開発スピードが速い中国の新興メーカーなども台頭し、足元では業界全体で協力を模索する事例も目立ち始めていた。

title: SA・PAのゴミ箱 280カ所で廃止へ
body: NEXCO東日本、NEXCO中日本、NEXCO西日本、本四高速の4社は2026年11月18日、管内路線の休憩施設のうち、レストランや売店といった営業施設のないエリアでゴミ箱の運用を順次廃止すると発表しました。【画像】「ゴミ箱ナシ！」になるSA・PAを見る今回のゴミ箱の運用廃止について、4社は衛生管理の向上、不法投棄の抑止、そして利用者や従業員の安全確保が目的と説明しています。対象となるのは、4社が管理する全852か所の休憩施設のうち、すでにゴミ箱を撤去済みの施設を含む280か所。来年1月から順次撤去を進める方針です。4社によると、全国の高速道路の休憩施設におけるゴミの回収量は年間約2万トンにのぼり、これはゴミ収集車で換算すると約1万台分に相当する量だといいます。また、近年は家庭から持ち込まれるゴミや、アルコール類の空き缶などの不法投棄も増加。なかには注射器など、適切に処理をせずに廃棄した場合は法令に抵触するおそれのある医療系廃棄物も含まれるそうです。こうした高速道路外からの持ち込みゴミなどにより、特に行楽シーズンにはゴミ箱が溢れかえる状況が頻発。ゴミの管理や分別、処分に多くの時間と労力を要していました。なお、廃止にあたっては利用者の混乱を避けるため、対象施設では約1か月前から事前告知を行うほか、撤去後も当面のあいだは看板などで利用者への周知を図る計画です。また、営業施設のあるSAやPAではゴミ箱の運用を継続します。鉄道駅などでは近年、駅のゴミ箱の撤去が相次いでいますが、高速道路のSA・PAも家庭ごみの持ち込みなどが問題となっています。4社は「お客さまにはご不便をおかけいたしますが、今後も安全・安心・快適にご利用いただける休憩施設づくりに努め、持続可能な施設運営等に取り組んでまいります」とコメントしています。

title: Suica「紫のうさぎ」得票率51.7%
body: JR東日本は11月18日、Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターのデザインを「B案」（紫のうさぎ）に決定した。9月の一般投票では総数166万4399票のうち、86万152票（51.7％）を獲得。キャラクターの愛称は、本日から12月15日まで一般募集する。【画像】各キャラクターデザインの原案者氏名・プロフィール ※画像を開いてからクリックで拡大【お詫びと訂正】初出時、動物の名前に誤りがありました。お詫びして訂正いたします。原案者・世戸ヒロアキ氏によるコメントは以下のとおり。このたびは、新しいSuicaのキャラクターに選んでいただき、誠にありがとうございます。投票の段階からみなさまに多くの反響をいただき、大変驚くとともに、とても嬉しく思っています。このキャラクターには、JR東日本とともに新しく進化していくSuicaの可能性やそこに込められた想いを、色や形、仕草のひとつひとつに反映しました。また、その想いを一人でも多くのお客さまに届けられるよう、さまざまなシーンで埋もれることなく存在感を発揮できるキャラクターを目指し、丁寧に設計しました。SNSでファンアートが生まれるなど、すでに多くの方々とのコミュニケーションが生まれていることを、とても嬉しく感じています。そうした反響を通じて、制作に込めた想いが少しずつ伝わっているのかなと感じています。私は原案制作という立場ですが、これからは多くの方々の手によって、このキャラクターがさらに成長し、皆さまに親しまれていくことを、皆さまと一緒に楽しみにしています。新キャラクターの選考は、JR東日本グループの経営ビジョン「勇翔2034」で掲げる“Suica Renaissance”の推進にあわせて進められてきたもの。Suicaをこれまでの「移動と少額決済のデバイス」から、利用客や地域と幅広くつながる「生活のデバイス」へ進化させる世界観を体現し、その象徴となるキャラクターとして位置づけられる。一次選考は2026年2月に発足した選考委員会が担った。JRグループ社員から寄せられた1万件を超える新キャラクターへの期待を踏まえ、委員会が指名した若手クリエイターが原案を制作。20弱の原案から3案に絞り込み、9月8日に候補を公開して、同日から23日まで特設サイトで一般投票を実施した。候補となった3案は次のとおり。A案：リス頭から尻尾まで一本のラインでつながる模様が特徴で、この線は鉄道から着想を得たというB案：紫のうさぎ安心を象徴する青と、感動を象徴する赤が混ざり合って生まれる色をまとうC案：ポシェットにモグラを入れた、オレンジの子土のなかしか知らないモグラにさまざまな景色を見せようという姿勢で、お出かけのワクワクを表現。オレンジの子は、何の動物かはあえて分からないようにされている選考委員会は、放送作家・脚本家の小山薫堂氏が座長を務め、委員はモデルの市川紗椰氏、イラストレーター/キャラクターデザイナーのきはらようすけ氏、デザイナー/アーティストの篠原ともえ氏、アニメ作家/キャラクターデザイナーのしまぐちニケ氏、声優/俳優の津田健次郎氏、クリエイティブディレクターの水野学氏。選考では「長く愛されるキャラクターになり得るか」「幅広い層が共感できる多様性を持つか」「そのキャラクターの豊かな物語を想像できるか」を重視したとしている。選考委員会座長・小山氏によるコメントは以下のとおり。みなさまから150万票以上というたくさんの投票をいただいた結果、ついにSuicaの新キャラクターが決定しました。しかしこの子の本当の物語が始まるのは、ここからです。どういう愛称で呼ばれ、どんな性格のキャラクターとして成長していくのか？　みなさまとともに創り上げていこうと思います。暮らしに寄り添うかけがえのない存在として、多くの人に愛され、どんな物語が描かれることになるのか？　未来のワクワクを一緒に紡ぎましょう！本日のデザイン発表にあわせて、新キャラクターの愛称の募集も始まる。愛称は2027年1月に選考委員会が審査し、同年3月31日のバトンタッチ式で発表する。

title: 賃上げより手取り増 食事補助注目
body: 物価高騰が家計を直撃し、働く人々にとってランチ代のやりくりは切実な悩みだ。東京都心では外食で1000円超えが常態化した。そんな中、企業の福利厚生として食事補助サービスが注目を集めている。【ひと目でわかる】「現金支給」と「食事補助」の比較　同額の賃上げよりも家計の助けに■物価高に嘆く働く世代都内で勤務する人々に、昼休みのランチ事情を聞いてみた。「1000円超えを『少し高いな』と感じたのは過去の話。今では1200～1500円が当たり前になった」と50代男性。安ければ五百円玉1枚だった時代も振り返りつつ「現金だけでなくキャッシュレス決済も増え、後から利用履歴を見て額に驚く」と嘆く。20代の梅村亮輔さんは「貯金のため上限を決め、クーポンを駆使する」。ほかにも「外食は高すぎるため、お弁当を持参する」と話す女性が複数いた。リクルート（東京）が運営する「ホットペッパーグルメ外食総研」が3月、20～69歳の働く男女4444人に実施した調査で、ランチの種別で最多となったのは、手作り弁当など「自炊または家族が作った食事」が30.6％で平均予算は439円。対して「出前・デリバリー」は1472円、「外食」は1338円で、いずれも前年より高額となった。■非課税枠で賢く手取り増そんなランチ代の高騰に「救いの一手」となる税制改正が今年、あった。企業が社員の食事代を非課税で半額補助する「食事補助」の上限が「月額3500円」から「月額7500円」に引き上げられた。これまでは昭和59年の設定当初の額が据え置かれたままだった。企業による食事補助は、同額の賃上げよりも家計の助けとなる。理由は、税金や社会保険料の仕組みにある。仮に企業が月額7500円を基本給の引き上げに充てれば、所得税や住民税、社会保険料も増える。一般的な会社員の場合、額面の2、3割が控除されるため、手元に残る増額分は月5000円前後にとどまる計算だ。一方、一定の条件を満たす現物支給の食事補助であれば、こうした税や保険料の負担増につながらない。企業が負担した7500円が実質、食費の足しになる。企業にとっても、社会保険料の会社負担分を抑えながら社員満足度を高められるという利点がある。■税制改正で導入増える

title: Suica新キャラ A案とC案も活用へ
body: JR東日本は18日、都内で「Suicaのペンギン」卒業に伴う新キャラクターのお披露目会を開催。新たなイメージキャラクターの原案候補3案の中から新キャラクターは、紫の「うさぎ」のB案に決まった。JR東日本の喜勢陽一社長はA案とC案も事業で活用する方針をサプライズで発表した。【写真】新キャラクターに選ばれたのは…大きな耳が特徴のSuica新キャラクター2001年のSuica導入時からのイメージキャラクターを担ってきた「Suicaのペンギン」は、2027年3月31日に卒業し、4月1日から新たなイメージキャラクターにバトンタッチする。選考委員が推薦した若手クリエイターに原案制作を委嘱。8月末に選考委員会を実施し、「Suica Renaissance」が目指す世界観などを踏まえ、新たなイメージキャラクターの原案候補を3案に絞った。A案はリスのキャラクター、B案は未来へ跳び進む紫の「うさぎ」、C案はなんの動物かいまいち分からない「オレンジの子」だった。特設サイトで投票が行われ、「お客さまからの投票を集約し、得票数が最も多いキャラクターをSuicaの新たなイメージキャラクターとして決定します」とし、結果発表はSuica誕生25周年となる2026年11月18日に実施された。候補3案について、2026年9月8日から23日の期間に投票を受け付け。総投票数166万4399票のうち、86万152票を獲得した「B」案に決定した。なおきょうから12月15日までの期間、B案のキャラクターの「愛称」を募集。選考委員会が決定し、2027年3月31日のバトンタッチ式にて発表となる。また、質疑応答でサプライズも。喜勢社長は「A案とC案、この2つも甲乙つけがたいぐらいお客様から得票をいただいた。ここで消えてしまうのはさみしい気がしています。A案とC案は私どもの事業活動の中で何かの活躍できるステージがないか考えております。A案とC案もお目に掛かることがあると思います」と発表した。■選考委員会メンバー小山薫堂氏（座長：放送作家／脚本家）市川紗椰氏（モデル）きはらようすけ氏（キャラクターデザイナー／イラストレーター）篠原ともえ氏（デザイナー／アーティスト）しまぐちニケ氏（アニメ作家／キャラクターデザイナー）津田健次郎氏（声優／俳優）水野学氏（クリエイティブディレクター／クリエイティブコンサルタント）

title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
summary: Watch: The BBC's Jonathan Beale joins Ukrainian forces taking the battle below ground and out of sight of Russian drones.
body:
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.
Read Jonathan Beale's dispatch from the front line.

title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
summary: Ukrainian forces are fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet tunnel in the Kharkiv region.
body:
Watch: Inside the gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
Troops move through the tunnel on special sleds - they call it the Kupyansk metro
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
Ukrainian troops like Musician rarely see the sun - but they say they feel safer underground
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
The men live and fight in very tight quarters - but have managed to clear 15km of the pipe
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".
There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.
It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
summary: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
body:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups anda United Nations fact-finding mission,external.
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military's operations in 2017
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
Aung San Suu Kyi's refusal to condemn the Myanmar military's actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.
The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.
Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."
He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.
Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.
Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

title: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for stock market debut worth up to $1.5tn
summary: Anthropic started just five years ago an is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has quickly become a big name in the tech industry
Anthropic is poised to hit avalue of up to $1.5tn (£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.
It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which facesquestions over whether the huge investmentpoured into the technology will be profitable.
The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world'smost highly valued stock debutwhen it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX sharesfell significantly in price.
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceXraised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollarsin financial obligationscome due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouringhuge amounts of moneyinto the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by agroup of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
Itrefused to complywith a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present athreat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Claude is Anthropic's widely-used AI chatbot
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent oncontroversial data centresand funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
summary: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.
body:
Sotheby's staff handle the "Châtaigniers en fleurs" painting by Vincent van Gogh at an auction preview in Hong Kong last month
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).
The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

title: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
summary: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
body:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.
So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.
It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.
Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.
Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".
The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.
It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.
"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.
Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?
"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.
There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.
With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.
Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.
Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts
Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.
While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.
That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.
But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.
"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."
Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.
"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."
Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
body:
Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.
At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco,impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.
Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.
His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
body:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO wasthe election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk wasspeaking virtually,externalat the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governorpromised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According toBBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
summary: A former McDonald's worker calls on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees” as a judge rules a legal case against the chain can go ahead.
body:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.
Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.
Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.
McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."
The latest developments come aftera BBC investigationin 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.
Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.
McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims
McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'
Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse
Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.
She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.
"I got the hell out of there," she says.
Ex-McDonald's worker: "You need to fix it so it doesn't happen again"
Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.
Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".
Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.
"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.
"And why would you? That is literally a child still."
Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.
The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.
The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.
Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.
Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".
"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it  a lot safer, I think, as well.  And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''
She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.
"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"
The claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.
The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.
Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard."
A McDonald's spokesperson said they could not comment on the specifics of ongoing legal proceedings.
In a statement, they said the company had "embedded an extensive set of robust and far-reaching initiatives" as part of its "steadfast commitment" to its staff, adding that this work continues.
"Any form of harassment, discrimination or inappropriate behaviour is unacceptable and has no place in our restaurants or offices. We are confident that with the guidance and partnership of external experts, we and our franchisees have industry leading safeguarding measures in place," the spokesperson added.

title: Google rejects UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
summary: This comes after Brand's wife shared a message from him in which he claimed his innocence.
body:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.
The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
There was no immediate comment from Google when approached by BBC News.
On Sunday, his wife Laura had shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a handwritten message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.
The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.
Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.
Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, saidshe found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting"and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.
She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.
Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".
In 2023,YouTube suspended Brand's channels from making money from advertsfor "violating" its "creator responsibility policy", shortly after he was accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013.
The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site.
Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

title: Lammy urges Burnham to take UK back into the EU
summary: The former deputy PM's intervention comes after Burnham reopened a debate over the UK's long-term future.
body:
David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to take Labour into the next general election with a pledge to rejoin the European Union.
The former deputy prime minister's intervention comes as Burnham prepares to explain how he sees the UK's long-term relationship with Europe developing.
Burnhamconfirmed on Tuesdayhe plans to set out his options next month, in the wake of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
Former business secretary Peter Kyle echoed Lammy's call to rejoin, meaning four former ministers from Sir Keir Starmer's cabinet have now publicly supported reversing Brexit in recent weeks.
The prime minister has held out the possibility he could ask to rejoin at some stage, whilst ruling out major changes before the next election.
Former chancellor Rachel Reevessaid earlier this monthshe believed "Britain's future lies in the European Union", following ex-Welsh secretary Jo Stevens in saying she wanted the UK to become an EU member again.
Neither specified a timeframe for the move, with Reeves insisting it was important to "get the next steps right".
But Lammy has now gone further, calling for Burnham to advocate rejoining at the next election, paving the way for a negotiation on a deal to return.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he added that the public should then be given a vote on whether to accept the new membership deal.
Returning to the bloc's customs union, in which EU member states charge the same taxes on imported goods, would not deliver "enough" economic growth, he said.
He added that rejoining Europe's single market from the outside was "not a runner" as it would mean applying swathes of EU law without a say on the content.
Another cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer, Peter Kyle, has also backed this approach,writing on Substack,externalearlier that a "complex halfway option" would be "the worst of all worlds".
He added that a promise to rejoin at the next election, followed by a renegotiation and a referendum on the final terms, was the "only way through I see".
He added: "How would I vote? Well, I would want to see the deal before deciding. I want Britain back in the EU, but not at any cost."
Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
Lammy, who is also a former foreign secretary, argued the UK would be able to rejoin the EU whilst staying outside the passport-free Schengen travel zone and without committing to adopt the euro.
But he appeared to concede that Britain's EU budget rebate, first negotiated in the 1980s, could become less financially generous, adding that a "different formula" for financial contributions would be "up for negotiation".
He also revealed he had made an unsuccessful attempt to persuade Sir Keir to "tear up" his red lines on Europe towards the end of his two-year premiership, but the former prime minister had encountered resistance from within his cabinet.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto committed the party to "make Brexit work" whilst ruling out rejoining either its customs union or single market.
Any move away from those red lines by Burnham would set up a huge dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at the next election.
But Lammy argued the prime minister's status as a former mayor from the north of England meant he was "uniquely placed" to convince the public of the need to reverse the decision to leave.
It comes as Burnham prepares to travel to the Brussels this Friday for an EU summit at which both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.
The prime minister inherited negotiations on those deals from his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who kicked off talks on the agreements last year.
But he has also started a broader discussion over the UK's long-term relationship with Europe, which has been welcomed by some within his own party but seen him accused by critics of betraying the result of the 2016 decision to leave.
Burnham's Conservative predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has urged the Labour leader not to start a renewed debate over EU membership.
Speaking last week, he warned a fresh debate over the issue would be "long and painful" and could harm attempts to improve upon the exit deal negotiated under the Conservatives.
He added: "The EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

title: Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
summary: The prime minister tells the BBC he wants to get "stuck in" after the Milburn report proposes wide-ranging changes to help unemployed young people.
body:
'I know actually what does work': Burnham unveils 45-day work placement plan for young people
The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.
Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."
Milburn'sreport,externalurged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.
The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".
"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.
Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.
Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."
He said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."
However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".
"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."
Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".
He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.
Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
Milburn says his proposals could save as much as £13.8bn in welfare costs over the next 10 years.
But after the extra spending on support for young people is taken into account,they are only projected to save £200m a year of taxpayers' money overall by 2036.
During Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch challenged Burnham over how long the plans would take to produce savings.
"[The prime minister] isn't planning any savings for 10 years," the Conservative leader said.
"We can't wait 10 years. Those young people need those jobs now."
Burnham insisted he would work "as quickly as possible to get the welfare bill down".
The prime minister added that he had asked the cabinet to "reprioritise spending plans" for next year to start funding new work placements for young people.
Accusing the Conservatives of a "cuts-only approach", he said: "The Milburn report says to reduce the welfare bill, you have to improve support."
Meanwhile, the government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.
The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".
College funding in England is lagged, so colleges receive money every September for the students they enrolled in the previous September.
Colleges say more teenagers in the population and greater demand for vocational courses means they currently either take on more students than they receive funding for, or they have to turn students away.
However, the DfE does not collect data on how often this happens or how many of those students end up among the 150,000 16 to 18-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's plans help you?
At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report
Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036
In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.
"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".
On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."
Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.
He also defendedhis reset with the EU,which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.
He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.
Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.
So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.
Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.
Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.
"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.
Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
summary: In her decision, Judge Emma Kelly says there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.
body:
The injunction granted by the High Court prevents Ryan Bridge and Raise the Colours from attaching flags and other items to public property
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.
The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.
Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.
Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.
In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.
The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.
It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.
The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.
The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.
Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.
The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he wasstruck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.
The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire,where the county council secured a permanent injunctionagainst four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.
Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge had argued an injunction would breach the European Convention on Human Rights
Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.
His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.
In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.
"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.
"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.
"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."
She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.
The council said anyone who breaches the injunction could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court
The injunction covers all unauthorised flags attached to street furniture, regardless of the type of flag involved.
Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, welcomed the ruling and described it as an "important step" in tackling unauthorised attachments to public highways.
She said residents remained free to display flags on their own property and said the council's approach had been "proportionate and evidence-led".
Councillor Jane Baston called the interim injunction an "important step" for the authority
Councillor Robert Alden, leader of Birmingham local Conservatives, criticised the authority's decision to pursue the injunction, saying it should focus on resolving the city's bin strike and improving basic services.
Campaign group Brummies United Against Racism & Hate Crime welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a welcome decision and long overdue".
A further hearing is due to take place in Birmingham on Thursday.
